subject: biology-hl
topicLabel: C1.2 — Cell respiration & D1.2 — Protein synthesis (Feb–Mar unit)

cards.back: Universal energy currency — hydrolysis to ADP + phosphate releases small, manageable packets of energy for every cell process.
glucose + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O (+ ATP). Photosynthesis is the same equation reversed.

cards.front: Three stages of aerobic respiration and their locations?
cards.back: Glycolysis — cytoplasm · Krebs cycle — mitochondrial matrix · oxidative phosphorylation (ETC) — inner membrane (cristae). Location questions are near-guaranteed.
Glucose (6C) → 2 pyruvate (3C); net 2 ATP + 2 NADH. Does NOT require oxygen — it predates aerobic respiration.
Terminal electron acceptor at the END of the ETC: combines with electrons + H⁻ → water. Without O₂ the ETC backs up and stops.
Animals: pyruvate → lactate (muscle fatigue). Yeast/plants: pyruvate → ethanol + CO₂. Both regenerate NAD⁺ so glycolysis can continue.

cards.front: Why does anaerobic respiration release so little ATP?
cards.back: Only glycolysis runs (≈ 2 ATP) — glucose is not fully oxidized, so most energy stays trapped in lactate or ethanol.

cards.front: Respirometer — what does the fluid movement measure, and why add KOH?
cards.back: Respiration absorbs O₂ and releases CO₂; KOH absorbs the CO₂, so the only gas change is O₂ decrease → fluid moves toward the organism. Rate of movement = respiration rate.

cards.front: Why keep the respirometer in a constant-temperature water bath?
cards.back: Respiration rate depends on enzyme activity (temperature-sensitive), and gas expansion from heat would confound the O₂ reading. Controls = design marks.
ETC pumps H⁻ into the intermembrane space; protons flow back through ATP synthase → ATP. Cristae (folds) maximize surface area → more ATP synthase.
Hydrogen carriers: collect electrons/hydrogen in glycolysis and the Krebs cycle, deliver them to the ETC.
RNA polymerase binds the promoter, unwinds DNA, uses one strand as template, joins RNA nucleotides into mRNA (5′ → 3′) — in the nucleus of eukaryotes.
Ribose sugar (vs deoxyribose) · uracil (vs thymine) · usually single-stranded (vs double helix).
Codon = 3-base triplet on mRNA; anticodon = complementary triplet on tRNA. Ribosome base-pairs them and joins amino acids with peptide bonds.

cards.front: Two properties of the genetic code and why each matters?
cards.back: Universal (same codons in nearly all organisms → human genes work in bacteria) and degenerate (several codons per amino acid → buffers point mutations).
AUG = methionine + start signal. UAA, UAG, UGA = stop codons — they code for NO amino acid and release the polypeptide.

cards.front: What happens to pre-mRNA before it leaves the nucleus?
cards.back: Splicing: introns (non-coding) removed, exons (coding) joined → mature mRNA. Bacterial mRNA needs no splicing.

cards.front: Why is the mitochondrial inner membrane folded into cristae?
cards.back: More surface area for the ETC and ATP synthase → more chemiosmosis → more ATP. Structure–function link, classic exam point.
Anticodon loop (3 bases) pairs with the mRNA codon; the 3′ end carries ONE specific amino acid — specificity at both ends guarantees correct sequence.
